About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Dance Years 11–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.
Progress and assessment information for Dance Years 11–13 is still in development.
Once that is completed, Dance Years 11–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister
of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the
Education and Training Act 2020.
It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Dance Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from 1
January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.
This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.




Dance | Years 11–13 | October 2026                                                   Page 2

Purpose statement
                                                                                      Te toi whakairo, ka ihiihi, ka wehiwehi, ka   Artistic excellence makes the world sit up
                                                                                      aweawe te ao katoa.                           in wonder.




 In Dance, students are taught dance through choreography, performance,
 responding to dance, and dance making. Students are taught literacy in dance as
 they examine dance elements, vocabularies, processes, principles, and
 technologies related to dance across diverse purposes, contexts, and forms.
 Students develop an understanding of how they can use their bodies to
 communicate ideas and meaning.

Students are taught the concepts, terminology, structures, and frameworks used in
dance, and how movements, choreography and performance communicate ideas,
intention, and meaning.
Dance provides students with the knowledge and practices to create, perform,
analyse, interpret, and evaluate dance works. This disciplinary knowledge helps
students develop expertise in using dance elements and vocabulary, choreographic
principles, and performance practices to communicate meaning and connect with
audiences.
As students progress through Years 11–13, they are taught to develop the capability
to analyse dance works, apply choreographic principles, evaluate creative and
performance decisions, and communicate informed perspectives using disciplinary
dance language.

 Dance leads to pathways in choreography, performance, research, and related
 areas such as creative arts, design, movement practices, arts administration,
 education, movement therapy, and cultural, social, or historical studies.

 Disciplinary Writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.
 In Dance, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to construct and justify interpretations, evaluations, and informed perspectives about dance works and practices using
 evidence and precise dance-specific terminology.

Responsible use of AI
Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative
processes, but it may also introduce bias, inaccuracies, ethical concerns, and issues
relating to ownership. AI should enhance, not replace, critical or creative thinking,
source evaluation, subject knowledge, or students’ own analysis and decision-
making. Responsible AI use emphasises the importance of exercising independent
judgement, drawing on credible sources, verifying information, being transparent
about AI use, considering diverse perspectives, and developing independent thinking.
In Performing Arts, where students use AI-assisted processes, they should critically
evaluate and direct their use of those tools, maintain ownership of creative decisions,
and ensure that creative works reflect their own artistic intent, experimentation, and
creative development.
Collaboration, collective responsibility, and safe practice
Creating dance is a relational process that balances individual agency with collective
responsibility. Through shared creative processes, and collaborative decision-making,
dancers develop relationships that support the creation, refinement, and realisation of
dance works. Concepts of Mahi ngātahi, manaakitanga, and whanaungatanga
underpin these processes and foster connection, shared leadership, and collective
responsibility.
Students should be taught to apply concepts of mahi ngātahi, manaakitanga, and
whanaungatanga by contributing and responding to ideas, making shared decisions,
and working respectfully with others. They should learn how to sustain personal and
collective responsibility throughout the choreographic process, collaboratively
generating, developing, refining, and integrating ideas.
